assessmentSummary.identity: A maximal or near-maximal linear acceleration effort over 10 yards from a specified start, ending with a planned safe run-out.
currentCardFindings: The current definition has no controlled movement patterns, body regions, constraints, load profile, fatigue profile, or difficulty scores.
A maximal-acceleration identity belongs primarily in output, not capacity. Repeated submaximal sprint conditioning requires a separate delivery profile with explicit intensity and density.
The current generic quality gate and 60-second rest default do not adequately protect maximal-speed quality across populations.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Use as fresh output work with full recovery and a clear run-out. Treat start type, stance, and small distance changes as variants or dosage modifiers; do not turn maximal efforts into conditioning by shortening rest.

evidence.sourceTitle: Correlations between muscle-tendon parameters and acceleration ability in 20 m sprints
claims: Rapid acceleration in the first sprint steps is a distinct performance quality in track and team sports.
Short acceleration performance depends on producing forward acceleration rather than maintaining maximal velocity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: The sprint start, push-off, and first acceleration steps are related but biomechanically distinguishable phases.
The card should be classified as linear locomotion and acceleration output, with the selected start recorded as a variant.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint Acceleration Mechanics: The Major Role of Hamstrings in Horizontal Force Production
claims: Sprint acceleration involves rapid hip, knee, and ankle actions with high lower-limb force and swing demands.
Hamstring contribution is important to horizontally oriented force production during acceleration.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Higher-performing initial acceleration is associated with greater propulsive force and forward-directed impulse.
The early steps progressively increase step length while the athlete rises from a forward projection; forced universal step positions are not supported.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: The first steps require high propulsive force, rapid limb exchange, and a transition from a projected start into cyclic sprinting.
Difficulty depends on start type, intent, athlete sprint competency, surface, and available run-out rather than distance alone.

evidence.sourceTitle: Correlations between muscle-tendon parameters and acceleration ability in 20 m sprints
claims: Power output is greatest in the first steps of sprint acceleration.
The card should track high neural intent, lower-limb tissue exposure, high-speed contacts, and performance drop-off rather than external load alone.
Sprint training requires an appropriate surface, marked distance, and sufficient space beyond the timing line.
Start type, footwear, surface, athlete readiness, and coaching visibility should be controlled before maximal efforts.
Acceleration and maximal-velocity training are programmed as quality sprint exposures with recovery selected to retain speed and technique.
Sets, distance, intensity, and rest should be explicit; repetition count alone does not define the sprint dose.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: The start should support rapid hip extension and forward propulsion without prescribing one anthropometrically inappropriate stance.
Early acceleration should emphasize force directed backward into the ground, progressive projection, and an uninterrupted run through the finish.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Youth training should be supervised, technically appropriate, and progressed from manageable demands.
Stop criteria should include pain, limping, unsafe surface or run-out, repeated stumble, and observable speed or posture loss.
Acceleration work is technically and physiologically distinct from maximal-velocity sprinting.
Maximal short sprints should be placed while the athlete is fresh; a dense repeated-sprint objective must explicitly reduce intensity or become a separate conditioning profile.
Acceleration develops incrementally across steps rather than through an instant upright sprint position.
Athlete-facing cues should focus on the task and projection while avoiding rigid promises about an identical stride pattern.
Coaches should distinguish acceleration from maximal velocity and select drills and recovery for the targeted quality.
Timing, video, or consistent split landmarks can support decisions, but technique and safe completion remain quality gates.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Speed tasks should be developmentally appropriate and built on movement competency.
Intent, distance, start complexity, footwear, and recovery can be adjusted without treating every short run as a maximal test.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Block, standing, three-point, falling, and other starts alter setup and the initial force task while retaining short acceleration as the central stimulus.
Flying sprints emphasize maximal velocity and should not be collapsed into a 10-yard acceleration identity.

alternateAssessments.rationale: The start position changes setup and initial force orientation while retaining the same short-acceleration stimulus.

alternateAssessments.name: Falling-Start 10-Yard Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: The falling start supplies a projection constraint and changes initiation without changing the primary acceleration identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Resisted 10-Yard Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: External resistance materially changes equipment, load, and force-velocity emphasis but remains a short acceleration task.

alternateAssessments.name: Flying 10-Yard Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: A flying entry targets maximal velocity after a build-up, not acceleration from a start, and needs different mechanics, space, dosage, and stop rules.
